challenges.name: pyramid-and-trophy-quiz
challenges.title: Which level should catch this bug?
challenges.description: Two decisions from the checkout team's test plan: where one bug should be caught, and what the pyramid and the trophy really say about end-to-end tests.

questions.explanation: Integration is right: the bug is in what the database does with the SQL, so a test must run the real query against a real (or local test) database with two or three orders and check their order. A static check (linter, type checker) only sees a valid string and a valid function; it knows nothing about the 'newest first' rule or what ORDER BY means. A unit test with a mocked db cannot catch it either: the mock returns whatever rows the test gives it, in whatever order, so the test checks the mock instead of the query. An end-to-end test through the browser would catch it, but it is not the lowest level: it needs the whole product running, takes seconds, and when it fails it points at a page, not at the query.

options.text: Static checks: a linter or type checker reading orders.repository.js
A unit test of listOrders with a mocked db whose query() returns three rows
An integration test that runs listOrders against a test database containing a few orders
An end-to-end test that logs in through the browser and reads the order-history page

questions.question: The team is redesigning the checkout suite that missed the VAT bug (about 180 browser tests, 42 minutes, red in about 6% of runs for unrelated reasons). Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: True: both the pyramid (Mike Cohn) and the trophy (Kent C. Dodds) keep end-to-end tests to a small top layer; they disagree on whether unit or integration tests form the bulk. True: a test that fails often for reasons unrelated to the change teaches people to ignore red, so a real failure is ignored too - that is what happened with the nightly report. False: the trophy still has a unit layer (and a static base); it only says integration tests should be the largest layer. False: e2e tests are slower and flakier because of what they run - a browser, servers, a database, the network and third-party pages - not only because of how they are written. Good selectors reduce flakiness but cannot make a multi-second browser journey as fast or as stable as a function call.

options.text: Both the test pyramid and the testing trophy keep end-to-end tests to a small layer at the top.
The testing trophy says to replace unit tests with integration tests completely.
A test that is red in about 6% of runs for unrelated reasons can do harm: people learn to ignore red, including real failures.
End-to-end tests are only slow and flaky when they are written badly; with good selectors they are as fast and stable as unit tests.
